title: Accessible Ice Cream: New England, at our family’s pace.
summary: Our new ice cream series begins at Rancatore’s in Lexington and Dairy Joy in Weston: firsthand family stories, picture-based choices and practical questions for your own visit.

title: A scoop, a phone, and a choice.
summary: An ordinary ice cream outing at Rancatore’s in Lexington, a real flavor-case photo and a family-made choice board. Practical ideas for families and independent scoop shops.
search: The journal / Lexington, Massachusetts / Family outings A family field note · Rancatore’s, LexingtonA scoop, a phone, and a choice.At Ranc’s, we photographed the flavor case and tried a picture-based way to show James the options. Here’s what we made—and what another family or scoop shop could take from it.By An AUsome LifeOctober 7, 2026Lexington, MA Our real photographAn ice cream cone, a brick-lined passage, and a photograph from our Lexington outing. The place: Rancatore’s, 1752 Massachusetts Avenue, Lexington. Check the shop’s current information or read our visit and parking notes.The resource: our own photo-to-choice experiment, plus free editable picture cards below. The illustrated board is an example from our outing—not today’s menu, a shop-provided service or evidence of a formal accessibility program.Originally published October 7, 2026. Practical family, retailer and sharing notes expanded October 19, 2026; this update does not describe a new visit. The choice belongs to the customerA case full of ice cream offers plenty to choose from. The question we brought to Ranc’s was how to put those choices in a form James could consider.We were heading to Rancatore’s in downtown Lexington—Ranc’s, as we call it—and I had my phone with me. James, my 14-year-old son, is autistic and non-speaking. He communicates in ways that include pointing and using his iPad, so clear pictures are part of our everyday life.We had already made a little visual board to choose where to go. Ranc’s, Cookie Monstah, and Wilson Farm each had their own picture. Once we reached the ice cream shop, there was another decision waiting for us: the flavors.Rather than try to recite the entire case out loud, I photographed the actual displays and shared them with AI. The idea was simple: bring the choices off the labels and onto a screen we could look at together.Our finished page was not a perfect menu or a finished communication system. It was a first attempt that needed checking. The photographs below show the source and the original result, including the parts we would simplify another time.We ended up with a photo just outside, an ice cream cone in hand. That ordinary afternoon—not the technology—is the point of the story.From the family notebookThe simple idea.A phone photograph can be a starting point. AI was one tool we tried for arranging the options; it is not a requirement.01Photograph the real, current options.02Show pictures the person recognizes.03Check, simplify, then leave room to choose—or decline.The support is new. James’s own communication methods are not.The practical version for another outing → A small experiment, right at the counterFrom the flavor case to the flavor board.These are the real photographs and the original combined choice board we made during our outing.01 / The source photographRealWe started with what was physically in the shop, not a generic ice cream menu.02 / The visual choice boardAIThe complete combined cone-and-flavor choice board from our outing, in its original arrangement. The AI-illustrated flavors still need checking against the actual case.The photographs document what we saw. The AI illustrations are an attempted translation, not independent confirmation of the labels, ingredients or choices available. Do not use this example as a current menu. A cup or a cone. Original editorial illustration. Before the ice cream counterFirst we chose where to go.We started with a visual destination board: Cookie Monstah in Burlington, Ranc’s in Lexington and Wilson Farm in Lexington. Each place had a familiar storefront picture rather than a generic picture of a cookie or an ice cream.Then, at Ranc’s, we made the combined cone-and-flavor board shown above. Its original layout keeps three cone choices at the top and the labeled flavors below. Another version could show these separately rather than presenting everything at once.The technology wasn’t making the choice for James. It was helping us show him the choices.Our original three-place destination storyboard, without redesigning it. A few things I learnedFast doesn’t mean finished.The AI was quick, but it wasn't automatically right. It can invent a flavor, misread a handwritten label, or make a beautifully crowded page. Our large flavor board was a first pass; a shorter display of the choices James wanted to consider might be easier to navigate.The real photos gave us something concrete to check. The board was never meant to replace James’s established augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) supports, or his ability to say no, ask for something different, or take a break.Sometimes the best visual is simply the photograph you already took. A picture cannot establish ingredients or allergen safety: ask staff about ingredients and cross-contact rather than inferring either from a label or illustration.An optional tool, not the whole methodA prompt to try.“Use these photos to make a draft picture choice board. Copy only labels you can read clearly, and flag anything uncertain instead of guessing. Do not add flavors, cone types or ingredient claims. Use clear labels and leave space to separate the flavor choice from the container choice.”A careful prompt is not a guarantee. Check every option against the current display and staff guidance before using the result. Remove unavailable items and change pictures or labels that do not suit the person.No AI needed: use a checked photo of a few actual options, or arrange your own photographs. Avoid capturing other customers or uploading private information. For your next scoopBring the choices closer. Keep the outing ordinary.This is what we would take from our Ranc’s experiment into another visit. Adapt the idea to the person—not the person to the board.Start with today’s options.Ask what is available, then use clear photographs or familiar pictures. Our old flavor board is a record of an experiment, not a shopping list for your visit. Check ingredients separately with staff.Make one question manageable.Try flavor and cup-or-cone as separate choices. Start with a manageable display while keeping a way to ask for other options. A shorter board should not silently remove the person’s right to choose something else.Leave time—and room for “no.”Keep the person’s usual communication available. Accept pointing, a device, speech or another familiar response without turning ordering into a test. Changing a choice, taking a break and declining are choices, too.Let a scoop be enough.Decide where eating will work and how to finish the visit. You do not need a second activity or a perfect photograph to make an ice cream stop worthwhile.Start with the free editable picture cards ↓These are family planning ideas, not an individualized communication assessment. It is whether a customer can find out what is available, take the time they need and communicate a choice in their own way.Keep choices current.A simple, current picture menu or clear photo of available flavors can be worth trying. Use readable labels, mark sold-out items and check information with staff. Pictures should not substitute for ingredient and allergy information.Welcome the customer’s tools.Address the customer, not only the person accompanying them. Make room for a phone, communication device or picture board, and ask what assistance would be useful rather than assuming.Offer another way to look.When feasible, let someone consider the choices away from the immediate ordering position without losing their opportunity to order. title: Tourists in Our Own Backyard
summary: A writer, a professor, and an overdue mid-fall date at Authors’ Ridge in Concord. Our photographs and watercolors, local history, a map, and practical access notes.
search: Concord, Massachusetts · Time for two Tourists in Our Own Backyard A mid-fall date at Authors’ Ridge. A writer, a professor, three years living nearby—and a little literary pilgrimage we somehow hadn’t made. Our photographs, watercolors, local history, and the practical details for a visit of your own. October 21, 2026 · An AUsome Life Louisa May Alcott’s resting place, from our own visit to Authors’ Ridge. I’m a writer. Dad is a professor. We’d lived here for three years.And somehow, we had never made the trek to Authors’ Ridge. On paper, we were very well qualified to have done this already. But a funny thing happens when you live near somewhere people travel to see: it becomes the place you can visit any time. And “any time” has a way of slipping behind everything that actually has a date on the calendar. So, for a little while this fall, we became tourists in our own backyard. Our date took us to Authors’ Ridge in Concord’s Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, where Louisa May Alcott, Henry David Thoreau, Nathaniel Hawthorne and Ralph Waldo Emerson are buried. Familiar names, suddenly attached to very small, very human places. About the writers and the cemetery. The things people leave behind Look closely at the photographs. Around Louisa May Alcott’s marker are pencils, pinecones, stones and a pink rose. At Thoreau’s, more pencils lie among the roots and needles, beneath a little stone that simply says Henry. I find the pencils especially moving. Such ordinary things, brought to the graves of people whose words have lasted so long. To me, they look like small thank-yous: your work reached someone. Someone is still reading. Hawthorne’s marker has its own quiet simplicity. A rounded stone, a surname, sunlight and shadow. You can know a name for years and still feel differently about it when you stand in front of it, outdoors, at the scale of a person. Henry: a small marker, tree roots, and the things visitors have left. Hawthorne, in patches of sun and shade. In our photographs, the trees still hold plenty of green. A little gold is beginning to show. The ground has its own autumn palette: brown needles, gray stone, moss, a bright flower. There is enough to look at before you read a single name. Before the graves, there were evening walks One of my favorite pieces of this place’s history is that the writers knew it as a place to walk. The National Park Service records that Emerson, Thoreau, and Nathaniel and Sophia Hawthorne enjoyed evening walks in Sleepy Hollow before it became a cemetery. Before these woods held their graves, they held their evening walks. That makes a date here feel part of a much older habit: going outside together, looking around, letting a familiar landscape give you something to think about. Sleepy Hollow was dedicated on September 29, 1855, with an address by Emerson. Landscape architects Horace William Shaler Cleveland and Robert Morris Copeland planned paths and drives around the natural shape of the land, respecting its trees and plants. The Concord Free Public Library’s dedication exhibit describes that approach—and notes that the place already carried the name Sleepy Hollow before it was a burial ground. It belongs to the nineteenth-century tradition of rural or garden cemeteries, where landscape and remembrance meet. The winding roads and wooded setting are part of the history you have come to see. Read about the landscape. A little more of the neighborhood Concord’s history reaches much further back than the writers. The Concord Museum identifies the area as the original homelands of the Nipmuc, Massachusett and Pawtucket tribal nations, and recognizes Indigenous people’s continuing connection to this land. Nearby, the North Bridge holds another chapter: the battle of April 19, 1775. A visit to Concord can open onto many histories. Authors’ Ridge gave us plenty to notice on its own. Something lovely, close to home A date like this makes room for the people we are as well as the people we look after. I’m still a writer. Dad is still someone who loves ideas. And we are still two people who can go somewhere together and find things worth noticing. I like that the visit didn’t need to be elaborate to be worth remembering. A nearby place, a little curiosity, a few photographs. There is a particular pleasure in finally doing the thing that has been waiting so close to home. Three years was a long time to get around to it. I’m glad we finally went. From the photographsA little autumn sketchbook Three watercolor interpretations of our visit. The photographs above show the actual places; these companion illustrations hold their color and feeling. About our editorial artwork. In mid-fall, plan around the earlier dusk. Check current town rules and posted gate signs. Mobility, ground surfaces & the approach Authors’ Ridge is a hillside visit. After rain, take extra care around wet leaves and roots. Restrooms & a place to regroup Plan a restroom stop in Concord Center. Outdoor space can still include other visitors, vehicles and maintenance sounds. If predictability helps, preview the photographs and town map, choose a short first stop, and keep an easy return to the car in your plan. If visiting with someone who uses AAC or other communication supports, keep their usual communication available and make room for “break,” “leave” and “all done.” For a date that depends on someone else covering care, our caregiver handover guide offers a place to put the essentials. Being a thoughtful visitor Sleepy Hollow is an active cemetery. Give funerals and people visiting loved ones plenty of space. Follow the roads and paths, respect the grave lots, and leave markers and existing objects undisturbed. The town prohibits gravestone rubbing. See the cemetery rules for the full visiting and photography guidance. Main Streets Market & Cafe at 42 Main Street is another nearby option for coffee or a meal. Check each business’s current hours and any access arrangements you need. These are ideas for extending your own outing. Or let the cemetery visit be the whole date. One nearby place, finally seen together, can be plenty. title: Old friends, an autumn wedding & a weekend away.
summary: An autumn wedding in New Haven, old college friends from Bristol and Rome, a little time away, and the grandparents who made it possible.
search: From the autumn camera roll · New Haven, Connecticut Old friends, an autumn wedding & a weekend away. College friends from Bristol and Rome, a wonderful wedding, a downtown hotel, and a little time to ourselves. A November 2018 memory · Shared October 22, 2026 All dressed up for a lovely autumn weekend. I've been loving all the old autumn photos that keep resurfacing on my phone lately. Every few days, another little memory pops up — a place we visited, people we love, or a wonderful weekend I'd nearly forgotten about. And these photographs from November 2018 took me right back to New Haven, Connecticut. We were there to celebrate the wedding of our dear friends Deb and Artur, and it was such a lovely excuse to reconnect with college friends from my years in Bristol, Rhode Island, and Rome, Italy. ❤️ There are some friendships that will always remind you of a particular time in your life — the places you went, the adventures you had, and the person you were back then. Seeing everyone again was such a treat. A sweet New England wedding detail, right down to the date on the maple-leaf bottle. A weekend away takes a village. Of course, leaving James for a weekend is never particularly easy for me. As many parents and caregivers know, even the loveliest getaway comes with a fair amount of planning (and perhaps a little worrying!). Thankfully, James was in wonderful hands with Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve, who love him beyond measure and have always been such an important part of our village. Knowing he was with people who know and adore him made it easier to enjoy a little grown-up time. ❤️ We stayed at the beautiful Omni New Haven Hotel at Yale, right downtown. It was such a treat to enjoy a lovely hotel, explore New Haven in autumn, catch up with old friends, and have a little time away from our everyday routines. And the New Haven pizza? Oh, my goodness. 🍕 That's a whole 'nother delicious story, and one that absolutely deserves its own post! Old friends, dressed for the occasion. A heartfelt family remembrance among the wedding details. Dessert, with a side of disco lighting. There may have been some spectacular fashion choices. And yes, the novelty hats came out. 😂 The people are the best part. Deb and Artur's wedding was beautiful, with heartfelt family tributes, wonderful food, lots of laughter, and some truly spectacular fashion choices once the novelty hats and oversized sunglasses made their appearance. But I think what I loved most was simply being together again. There is something so special about friendships that stretch across years, countries, and completely different chapters of life. The people who knew you when you were young and figuring everything out, and who still feel like old friends no matter how much time has passed. And as much as I love sharing adventures with James, these occasional grown-up getaways are part of our story, too. Being a caregiver is a huge part of my life, but so are the friendships, places, memories, and experiences that have helped make me who I am. One more thing worth rememberingGood people make room for good weekends. This getaway was possible because Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve could be there for James. That kind of trusted family support matters, and I never take it for granted. Not every family has it; it's one reason I believe time for caregivers, and real support to make it possible, is so important. I'm so glad these photos found their way back onto my phone this autumn. A lovely reminder of a beautiful weekend, two wonderful people, and friendships I'm very grateful to have made along the way. ❤️ Here's to Deb and Artur, old friends, and all the stories that follow us home. 🍁 Places & outings Travel & stays

title: A little Easter color.
summary: An Easter family visit to Berlin Farms in Massachusetts: colorful eggs, an enthusiastic bunny, wide-open fields and a few practical notes before you go.
search: The journalBerlin, MassachusettsAn Easter field note The bunny had a few photo ideas of its own. A spring visit to Berlin FarmsA little Easter color.An egg hunt, a bunny with a few good poses, and a family photograph worth keeping.An AUsome Life · Published October 7, 2026 From an earlier Easter visitPastel eggs across the lawn. White fences beyond the buildings. One orange jacket that had apparently declined the pastel dress code.Our Easter photographs from Berlin Farms deserved a little space in the journal. Opened from the family albumThe eggs were everywhere.There is a particular sort of New England spring photograph: green beginning to return to the grass, bare trees in the distance, and everybody sensibly still wearing a jacket. Our Berlin Farms pictures have all of that, with the addition of a lawn covered in pink, yellow, blue and green eggs.A canvas shopping bag is ready for the egg hunt. The Easter Bunny has a pink bow, a floral backdrop, and considerably more enthusiasm for posing than most adults can sustain. I especially like the photograph with the arms up. There is plenty happening in it, and that smile is the part I keep coming back to.Then there is the family picture: the three of us together, the bunny at one end, and the stone patio beneath our feet. I am glad we have that one. A canvas tote, a lawn full of eggs, and a very visible orange jacket.All of us in the frame. The bunny makes four. A little spring color. Original editorial illustration.Between the photographsA little room to look around.The farm makes a lovely setting for this chapter. White clapboard buildings sit beside lines of white fencing, with fields stretching beyond them. In one photograph, a horse is grazing in the distance. The colors are mostly green, white and gray, which leaves the orange jacket with very little competition.I like having a wider view among the close-ups. It brings back the shape of a place: the deck, the fence, the buildings around the egg-hunt lawn. A family album needs a little of the scenery, too.
